title: Guide Part 1: Read this first: what is realistic
text:
Your goal is one fast, strong, self-hostable AI that developers can build on. The route there is clear, but
three points will save you months if you accept them early.
You do not merge Gemma, Qwen and Kokoro into one network
These models have different architectures and jobs. Kokoro is a small text-to-speech model, Gemma and
Qwen are language (and in some versions multimodal) models. What you build is a system: several
specialist models behind one gateway with one API. To the developer it looks like one AI. Inside, a router
sends each request to the right model.
Fine-tuning shapes behaviour; it does not create frontier intelligence
Fine-tuning teaches a model your formats, tone, tools, domain knowledge and local context. It does not
add the broad reasoning of a model trained at frontier scale. The honest target is: best-in-class for your
chosen tasks at low cost and low latency, running on hardware you control. Pick the base model with
the strongest raw ability you can afford to host, then specialise it.
Data quality decides the result
With modern tools the training step is a few commands. The difference between a demo and a product is
the dataset: what you collected, how you cleaned it, and how you measured it. Part 4 is the longest section
on purpose.
Legal check before you collect anything. Every dataset and every base model has a licence. Many
commercial AI providers forbid using their model outputs to train competing models. Use open licensed data,
data you own, data with user consent, and outputs from models whose licence allows it. Keep a provenance
record for every source (Part 4.2).

title: Guide Part 3: Choosing base models
text:
Open-weight releases move fast. Treat the table as a starting shortlist and re-check Hugging Face
trending and each model card (licence, size, context length, benchmarks) the week you start.
Capability | Candidates to evaluate | Notes
General chat and
reasoning | Qwen 3.x family, Gemma 4, Mistral Small / | Gemma 4 and recent Qwen releases are
Coding and terminal | Ministral 3, DeepSeek (large, needs many | Apache-2.0 per the sources checked. Confirm
agent | GPUs) | on the model card.
Vision
Speech to text | Qwen coder-class models, strong general | Pick a model with native tool calling. Agent
Text to speech | Qwen/DeepSeek models with tool use | behaviour matters more than raw code
completion.
Image generation
Embeddings | Multimodal Gemma, Qwen-VL class models | Natively multimodal models fine-tune more
simply than bolting an encoder on yourself.
Whisper (large-v3 class), faster-whisper | Fine-tune when your accents or languages
runtime | score poorly.
Kokoro 82M (Apache weights, runs on CPU or | Fast and light, several languages. Built for
small GPU) | inference; for a brand-new voice or language
see Part 6.4.
Open diffusion models (SDXL / FLUX class) | Licences differ, some restrict commercial use.
Read before you ship.
BGE, E5 or GTE class | For retrieval over developer docs.
Selection rules
- Start with one strong general model (about 8B to 32B) before collecting many models. Add specialists
only when measurements show a gap.
- Prefer Apache-2.0 or MIT licences if developers will build commercial products on your work.
- Prefer Mixture-of-Experts models when speed matters: few active parameters per token means faster
inference and cheaper fine-tuning.
- Always compare the base model on your own test set (Part 9) before choosing. Public leaderboards
do not predict your tasks.

title: Guide Part 4: Data: collection and cleaning
text:
The rule: a small, clean, well-labelled dataset beats a large noisy one. Plan to spend about 60 to 70 percent of
the whole project on data. Plan the evaluation set first, because it tells you what data you actually need.

title: Guide Part 4.1: Define the task before collecting
text:
1 Write one sentence per capability: what input comes in, what output must come out, and what a perfect
answer looks like.
2 Write 20 to 50 example conversations by hand for each capability. These become your style guide and
seed data.
3 Define the output schema: chat template, tool-call JSON, emotion event JSON, transcript format.
4 Build the evaluation set first (Part 9), then keep it sealed. Never train on it.

title: Guide Part 4.2: Provenance and licensing record
text:
Create one table (a spreadsheet is fine) and fill a row for every source before it enters the pipeline.
Field | Why it matters
Source name and URL | Reproducibility and takedown handling
Licence | Decides whether commercial use is allowed
Date collected and version | Datasets change; you must know which version trained the model
Consent status (for user or voice data) | Privacy law and trust
Contains personal data? | Triggers the PII process in 4.5
Share-alike or attribution duties | Release obligations for your own model and data

title: Guide Part 4.3: Where data comes from
text:

Instruction and | Tulu 3 SFT mixture, SmolTalk, OpenAssistant | Real questions from your users and
chat | (OASST), FineWeb-Edu (knowledge text) | developers (with consent), support tickets,
docs, forum threads
Code | The Stack v2 (licence-filtered code), GitHub repos Your own repos, internal tools, recorded
you filter by licence, Stack Exchange dumps | terminal sessions
Terminal agent | Public agent-trajectory datasets, SWE-style task | Sessions recorded in sandboxes, with tests
sets | that confirm success
Vision | LLaVA-style instruction sets, DocVQA, ChartQA, | Screenshots of your product, diagrams, local
ShareGPT4V-type caption sets | documents, annotated photos

signed consent and transcripts
Speech (TTS) | Open single-speaker corpora with permissive | A voice actor you hire and contract: clean
licences | studio audio
Animation / | Emotion-labelled dialogue sets (small, then | Scripts you write: line, emotion, gesture,
emotion | expand) | intensity
Synthetic | Generate from strong open models whose licence Seed with your 20 to 50 handwritten
allows it | examples, then filter hard
If you target East African users, local languages and accents are an opportunity: Common Voice includes
Ugandan languages, and public models are weakest exactly there. A few hundred hours of clean local
speech can beat a much larger general model on your users.

title: Guide Part 4.4: The universal cleaning pipeline
text:
Run every text source through the same ordered stages. Log how many records each stage removes. If
one stage removes 50 percent, look at samples, because either the source or the filter is wrong.
1 Extract. Convert HTML, PDF, DOCX to clean text. Remove menus, cookie banners, footers. Use
trafilatura for web pages. For PDFs use a text extractor, and OCR only scanned pages.
2 Normalise. Fix encoding (ftfy), unify Unicode, collapse whitespace, repair broken line wraps, keep
code indentation untouched.
3 Language ID. Detect language per document (fastText). Keep the languages you support.
Mixed-language rows need a rule.
4 Heuristic quality filters. Drop too short or too long rows, rows with very high symbol ratio, repeated
lines, boilerplate, keyword-stuffed spam, and refusals like "As an AI I cannot" when you do not want
that behaviour.
5 Exact dedupe. Hash each normalised record and drop copies.
6 Near-duplicate removal. MinHash plus LSH (datasketch) on 5-grams, similarity threshold around 0.8.
Duplicates cause memorisation and inflate scores.
7 Model-based quality scoring. Score rows with a small classifier or an LLM judge using a rubric
(correct, helpful, well formatted). Keep the top slice. Spot-check 100 kept and 100 dropped rows by
eye.
8 PII and secrets scrub. Remove emails, phone numbers, national IDs, addresses, API keys,
passwords, tokens (regex plus a detector such as Presidio, and gitleaks for code). Replace with
placeholders.
9 Safety filter. Remove content you will not support (abuse, malware, sexual content involving minors,
targeted harassment). Keep a small, curated set of safe refusal examples so the model learns to
decline correctly.
10 Decontaminate. Remove any record that overlaps your evaluation set or public benchmarks (n-gram
overlap). Otherwise scores lie.
11 Format. Convert to the exact chat template of the base model, with system, user, assistant and tool
roles. Wrong templates silently ruin fine-tunes.
12 Split and version. Train, validation and sealed test split by source or conversation, never by random
row, to prevent leakage. Version with DVC or Hugging Face datasets and write a data card.

title: Guide Part 4.5: Modality-specific cleaning
text:
Instruction and chat data
- Check that the answer actually answers the question; drop rows where the assistant drifts, hedges
endlessly or contradicts itself.
- Verify facts you can verify. For maths, run the calculation. For definitions, spot-check against a trusted
source.
- Keep diversity: balance topics, difficulty, length, and languages. Cap any single template at a small
share, or the model learns the template.
- Multi-turn data: keep full conversations, and mask loss so the model trains only on assistant turns.
Code and terminal data
- Execute, do not just read. Run code and unit tests in a sandbox. Keep only samples that pass. For
terminal tasks, store the command, the real output, and the next action, and keep only trajectories
whose final check succeeds.
- Filter by repository licence. Remove generated files, minified code, vendored libraries and huge
auto-generated blobs.
- Remove secrets and internal URLs. Remove destructive commands (rm -rf, format, curl piped to shell)
from positive examples unless the example demonstrates asking for confirmation.
- Record tool-call format exactly as your agent will use it (JSON arguments, error handling, retries).
Vision data
- Drop corrupt, tiny or low-resolution images. Remove exact and perceptual duplicates (pHash, or CLIP
embedding similarity).
- Check caption quality: a caption must describe what is visible. Re-caption weak rows with a strong
open VLM, then sample-check.
- For documents and screenshots, verify OCR text against the image on a sample; wrong text teaches
hallucination.
- Remove faces and personal images without consent, unsafe imagery, and watermarked stock content.
- Keep question and answer pairs balanced: counting, reading text, charts, UI elements, spatial relations.
Speech data for STT (Whisper)
- Convert to 16 kHz mono WAV. Normalise loudness. Cut into segments of about 5 to 30 seconds using
voice activity detection (Silero VAD).
- Transcripts must match audio exactly: spelling rules, numbers, punctuation, code-switching. Write a
transcription guide and apply it to all labellers.
- Automatic quality filter: transcribe each clip with a strong pretrained model; if word error rate against the
human transcript is very high, the label or audio is bad. Review those.
- Remove clipped audio, music-heavy clips, very long silences, and speakers without consent.
- Balance speakers, genders, ages, accents, microphones and noise levels, so the model does not fail
on groups you under-sampled.
Speech data for TTS (new voice)
- Use a professional or well-trained speaker in a quiet room, one microphone, consistent distance. 10 to
50 hours of clean audio is the usual range for good single-voice quality; less can work for adaptation.
- Scripts: cover all phonemes and common names, numbers, abbreviations, questions, statements, and
emotional styles you want.
- Align text and audio (forced alignment, for example Montreal Forced Aligner), drop clips where
alignment fails.
- Get a signed voice contract. Never train on a voice without written consent.
Animation and emotion data
The face is a renderer, not a model. What you teach the LLM is to emit structured events alongside its
words, for example:
{"text": "Great question!", "emotion": "joy", "intensity": 0.7,
"gesture": "nod", "gaze": "user", "speak_style": "bright"}
- Write the schema first: a closed list of emotions, gestures, gaze targets, intensities. A closed
vocabulary is what makes this reliable.
- Create 2,000 to 10,000 labelled lines covering greetings, thinking, errors, celebration, confusion,
empathy, long explanations. Have two people label a sample and measure agreement.
- Lip-sync comes from TTS phoneme or word timing, not from the LLM. Store timing with each audio clip.
- Validate that every output parses as valid JSON against the schema. Drop rows that do not.

title: Guide Part 4.6: Quality gates before training
text:
Gate | Pass condition
Manual review | You read at least 200 random rows per source and per capability and judge 95 percent or
more acceptable
Dedupe report | Near-duplicate rate under a few percent; no train/test overlap
Distribution check | No topic, template or speaker dominates; length distribution looks natural
Format check | 100 percent of rows parse in the training template; tool and emotion JSON validates
Safety and PII | Scans return zero secrets; PII removed or masked; consent records exist for user data
Data card written | Sources, licences, filters, known gaps, date, version
Suggested data volumes (starting points, not rules)
Goal | Starting size | Comment
Style, format, persona, tool format | 1,000 to 10,000 high-quality | Quality dominates; hundreds can already
(SFT) | examples | shift behaviour
Domain skill (docs, API, local | 10,000 to 100,000 examples plus | Use RAG for facts that change; fine-tune
curriculum) | retrieval | for skills
Coding / terminal agent | 5,000 to 50,000 verified trajectories Verification by tests is worth more than
volume
Vision instruction tuning | 10,000 to 100,000 image-text pairs Many fewer if the base is already
multimodal
Whisper new accent or language | 50 to 500+ hours | Cleaner labels beat more hours
Preference tuning (DPO) | 2,000 to 20,000 chosen/rejected | Pairs must differ in quality for a real
pairs | reason

title: Guide Part 5.1: Which method
text:
Method | What it does | Use when
Prompting + RAG | Gives the model instructions and documents at Facts change often; first thing to try
request time
SFT (supervised fine-tuning) Trains on input to ideal output pairs | Teach format, tone, tools, domain
skills
LoRA / QLoRA | Trains small adapter matrices; QLoRA does it | Default choice: cheap, fast, keeps
on a 4-bit base | base ability
DPO / preference tuning | Trains on chosen vs rejected answers | Polish helpfulness, safety, style after
SFT
RL with verifiable rewards | Rewards answers that pass tests or checks | Code, terminal agents, maths, tool
(GRPO) | success
Distillation | Student model learns from a stronger teacher's Make a small fast model; check
outputs | teacher licence
Full fine-tune / continued | Updates all weights on large raw text | Only with large data and many GPUs;
pretraining | usually unnecessary

title: Guide Part 5.2: Tools
text:
- Unsloth: fast, low-VRAM LoRA/QLoRA, good for one GPU.
- LLaMA-Factory: web UI and config-driven training for many model families including multimodal, with
SFT, DPO and GRPO.
- Hugging Face TRL + PEFT + Transformers: the standard code-level stack.
- Axolotl: YAML-driven recipes for multi-GPU runs.
- DeepSpeed / FSDP: when the model does not fit on one GPU.
- Weights and Biases or MLflow: track every run; DVC for data versions.

title: Guide Part 5.3: Hardware guide (rough, with QLoRA)
text:
Model size | GPU memory to fine-tune | GPU memory to serve (4-bit to 8-bit)
4 to 8 GB
1B to 4B | 8 to 16 GB | 8 to 20 GB
20 to 40 GB
7B to 14B | 16 to 24 GB | 40 to 80 GB or multi-GPU
27B to 35B (dense or MoE) | 24 to 48 GB
70B and larger | 80 GB or multi-GPU
These are planning numbers. Long context, big batches and multimodal inputs raise memory use. Rent
GPUs by the hour for training (RunPod, Lambda, Vast.ai, a hyperscaler, or your own cloud), then keep a
smaller always-on set for serving.

title: Guide Part 5.4: Safe starting hyperparameters for LoRA SFT
text:
Setting | Starting value
LoRA rank / alpha | 16 to 64 / equal to rank or 2x rank
Target modules | All linear layers (attention and MLP)
Learning rate | 1e-4 to 2e-4 for LoRA (about 10x lower for full fine-tuning)
Epochs | 1 to 3; stop when validation loss stops improving
Effective batch size | 32 to 128 sequences via gradient accumulation
Sequence length | As short as your data allows (2048 to 8192); pack short examples
Loss masking | Train on assistant tokens only
Precision | bf16 compute, 4-bit base weights for QLoRA
Replay data | Mix 10 to 30 percent general data to avoid forgetting
Always run a tiny overfit test first: 20 examples, many steps. If the model cannot memorise them, the
template, masking or learning rate is wrong.

title: Guide Part 6.1: Text assistant (the core model)
text:
1 Choose the base (Part 3) and read its chat template.
2 Assemble 5,000 to 50,000 cleaned examples: your handwritten set, filtered public data, curated
synthetic data.
3 Run SFT with LoRA (Part 5.4). Evaluate on your sealed set.
4 Collect failures, write better answers, add them, retrain. Two or three rounds beat one big run.
5 Run DPO on chosen/rejected pairs from your own model's outputs ranked by judge plus human
review.
6 Merge the adapter into the base weights, export safetensors, quantise (AWQ or FP8 for vLLM, GGUF
for llama.cpp), re-evaluate the quantised model.

title: Guide Part 6.2: Coding and terminal agent (Claude Code style)
text:
A terminal agent is a loop: read the situation, choose a command or edit, run it, read the result, continue.
You train the model to do this loop correctly, and you build the harness around it.
1 Pick a model with strong tool calling. Terminal ability depends on following structured tool formats.
2 Build the harness first. Tools: read file, write/edit file, run shell command (in a sandbox), search, ask
the user. Docker or gVisor isolation, timeouts, a command allowlist, and confirmation for destructive
actions.
3 Collect trajectories. Run a strong model (whose licence permits it) or human experts on real tasks in
the sandbox. Record every step: thought, tool call, tool output.
4 Verify. Keep only trajectories whose tests or checks pass. Also keep a small set of recovery examples
where the first command fails and the next one fixes it.
5 SFT on verified trajectories with loss on the model's actions only (not tool outputs).
6 RL (GRPO) with verifiable rewards. Reward = tests pass, minimal diff, no forbidden commands. This
step gives the biggest gain for agents.
7 Evaluate on held-out repositories and task suites; measure pass rate, steps taken, and
unsafe-command rate.

title: Guide Part 6.3: Vision
text:
1 Start from a natively multimodal base.
2 Freeze the vision encoder first; train LoRA on the language layers and the projector with image-text
instruction data.
3 Add your domain images (screenshots, diagrams, documents). Include questions of every type:
describe, read text, count, compare, locate, reason.
4 Evaluate with a custom set plus public sets (document QA, chart QA, general visual QA). Check for
hallucinated text in documents.
5 Serve with the same vLLM stack that serves the text model.

title: Guide Part 6.4: Speech
text:
Speech to text
1 Start from a Whisper checkpoint close to your size and latency budget.
2 Fine-tune with the Hugging Face sequence-to-sequence trainer on your cleaned 16 kHz segments.
3 Evaluate word error rate on a speaker-disjoint test set, per accent and per noise condition.
4 Serve with faster-whisper (CTranslate2) for speed; add streaming with VAD chunking.
Text to speech
Kokoro is a compact open-weight model built on a StyleTTS2-style design; the project is oriented to
inference and ships a set of voices. For most products, use it as-is. If you need a brand-new voice or a
language it lacks, check the current Kokoro repository for training support. Otherwise train a model that
has a documented training recipe (a StyleTTS2-based model, Piper, or XTTS-class models) on your clean
studio data (Part 4.5), and keep Kokoro as the fast default.

title: Guide Part 6.5: Animation like an emo robot
text:
1 Define the emotion and gesture vocabulary (Part 4.5).
2 Fine-tune the chat model so every reply includes the event JSON next to the text. Constrain decoding
to the schema (grammar or JSON mode in vLLM).
3 Stream: text tokens go to TTS sentence by sentence; events go to the renderer.
4 TTS returns audio plus word or phoneme timing; the renderer maps phonemes to mouth shapes
(visemes) and blends emotion poses on top.
5 Build the face in a real-time renderer (Rive, Lottie, WebGL or Unity). Idle animation, blinking,
micro-movements and easing curves create the movie feel, not the AI model.
6 Test with the emotion labels from your held-out set: does the face match the sentence?

title: Guide Part 6.6: Image generation
text:
Use an open diffusion model and train a LoRA for your style from 50 to 500 curated, captioned,
rights-cleared images. Check the base model licence for commercial use. Serve on a dedicated GPU
queue because generation is slow compared to chat.

title: Guide Part 7: Combining everything
text:
Option | How | Pros | Cons
A. One multimodal
model | A single natively multimodal base for Simplest to operate | One model must be good
B. Many LoRA | text, vision and code, with LoRA | at everything
adapters on one base
C. Model merging | vLLM multi-LoRA serves chat, code, Cheap: one set of base | Adapters share the same
persona adapters on one loaded base weights in memory | base ceiling
D. Separate models
behind a gateway | Merge fine-tunes of the same base | One file, no routing | Needs same architecture;
(mergekit: TIES, DARE, SLERP) | test for regressions
Router sends requests to specialists | Best quality per task, | More GPUs and more
easy to upgrade parts | moving parts
Recommended path: start with A plus B for language, vision and code, and use D for the models that are
different by nature: Whisper, Kokoro, diffusion and embeddings. Use C only for same-base fine-tunes,
after measuring.
Router design
- Version 1 uses rules: request contains audio, so STT; contains image, so VLM; route name /code, so
coder; otherwise chat.
- Version 2 adds a small classifier or the LLM itself to choose between fast and strong models: easy
questions to the small model, hard ones to the large model.
- Add fallbacks: if a backend times out, retry on another replica or a smaller model.
- Log every routing decision; use the logs to improve the router and to find new training data.

title: Guide Part 8.1: API surface developers expect
text:
Endpoint | Purpose
POST /v1/chat/completions | Chat, tools, vision (image parts in messages), streaming
POST /v1/audio/transcriptions | Speech to text (Whisper)
POST /v1/audio/speech | Text to speech (Kokoro) with streamed audio
POST /v1/images/generations | Image generation
POST /v1/embeddings | Embeddings for retrieval
WebSocket /v1/realtime | Live voice conversation and animation events
GET /v1/models | List models and capabilities
Copy the OpenAI-compatible request and response shapes. Every existing SDK and tool then works with
your gateway by changing only the base URL. This is the single biggest adoption decision you will make.

title: Guide Part 8.2: Components
text:
- vLLM for the LLM and VLM: continuous batching, paged attention, prefix caching, multi-LoRA,
speculative decoding, tensor parallelism.
- LiteLLM proxy (or your own FastAPI layer) in front: virtual keys, budgets, rate limits, logging, fallbacks,
routing between vLLM backends.
- faster-whisper and Kokoro as small services on CPU or a shared GPU.
- Redis for rate limits and caches, Postgres for keys and usage, Prometheus + Grafana for metrics.
- Docker for every service; add Kubernetes or Nomad when you have more than a few nodes.

title: Guide Part 8.3: Making it fast
text:
Roughly halves memory or better, raises tokens per second; always
Technique | re-run your eval on the quantised model
Quantisation (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) | Many users share a GPU efficiently
Continuous batching + paged KV cache | Reuses system prompts and long shared context
(vLLM) | A small draft model proposes tokens, the big model verifies: faster
Prefix caching | generation
Speculative decoding | Few active parameters per token: higher speed for the same quality
First token or first audio chunk arrives sooner; feels much faster
MoE models | Less prefill time and memory
Streaming everywhere | Memory bandwidth drives decoding speed; benchmark before buying or
Shorter prompts, smaller context | renting
Right-size the GPU
Latency budget for a talking robot (target under about one second to first sound)
Stage | Target
Voice activity detection and end-of-speech | 50 to 200 ms
Streaming speech to text final | 150 to 300 ms
LLM time to first token | 150 to 400 ms
TTS first audio chunk (sentence-level streaming) | 100 to 250 ms
Network and rendering | 50 to 100 ms

title: Guide Part 8.4: Deployment
text:
1 Start on one GPU server with Docker Compose: vLLM, gateway, Whisper, Kokoro, Redis, Postgres.
2 Put nginx or Caddy in front with TLS; require API keys; set per-key rate limits from day one.
3 Add a second node and replicate the vLLM service; let the gateway balance between them.
4 Keep a CPU-only fallback (a small quantised model through llama.cpp) so the service degrades
instead of failing.
5 Automate: build images in CI, push to a registry, roll out new model versions behind a canary
percentage.
6 Security: sandbox the terminal agent, never expose raw model ports, store secrets in a vault, log
without storing sensitive prompts unless users opt in.

title: Guide Part 9: Evaluation
text:
Evaluation is not the last step. You build it first, run it after every change, and refuse to ship when it
regresses.
Capability | Automatic measures | Human / custom measures
Chat and reasoning MMLU-style knowledge sets, | 200 to 500 golden prompts from real users,
instruction-following sets | rated on a rubric
Coding | HumanEval / LiveCodeBench-style tests, | Hold-out repositories, code review of samples
unit-test pass rate
Terminal agent | Task success rate, steps per task, unsafe | Replay of failed sessions
command rate
Vision | Document QA, chart QA, general visual QA | Your screenshots and documents;
scores | hallucination checks
STT | Word error rate per accent, noise level, speaker Listen to the worst 50 clips
group
TTS | Intelligibility (ASR round-trip), latency, real-time Listening tests (MOS-style) with real users
factor
Animation | Schema validity rate, emotion label accuracy | Does the face feel right? Short user study
System | p50 / p95 latency, throughput, error rate, GPU | Load tests at 2x expected traffic
cost per 1,000 requests
- Compare every candidate against the base model without fine-tuning and against the previous
version. Fine-tuning that does not beat the base is wasted.
- LLM-as-judge is useful and cheap, but calibrate it: check its scores against human ratings on 100
samples.
- Run safety red-teaming: jailbreaks, prompt injection through documents and web pages, harmful
requests, privacy leaks.
- Track regressions on general ability (forgetting). If general scores fall, add replay data or lower the
learning rate or rank.

title: Guide Part 10.1: Package
text:
- Weights in safetensors, plus quantised builds (GGUF, AWQ or FP8) so people can run locally or on
GPUs.
- A clear licence file for your weights and for any data you release. Say plainly what is allowed
commercially.
- A model card: intended use, training data summary, evaluation results, known limits, safety notes.
- A data card for any released dataset (Part 4.6).
- Docker images and a one-command start script for the whole gateway stack.

title: Guide Part 10.2: Developer experience
text:
- OpenAI-compatible API so existing code works unchanged.
- SDKs for Python and JavaScript, a quickstart that works in five minutes, and copy-paste examples:
chat, tools, vision, voice, the robot face.
- A playground web page, API reference, and a public changelog with version numbers
(model-name-v1.2).
- A free tier with rate limits, clear pricing for more, and a status page.
- A community channel and a feedback button inside every example.

title: Guide Part 10.3: Keep improving
text:
- Collect opt-in feedback (thumbs up/down, corrections). Corrected answers are your best future training
data.
- Review failures weekly, add them to the evaluation set, and retrain monthly or quarterly.
- Version everything: data, code, configs, model. You must be able to reproduce any released model.
- Publish honest benchmarks including weak areas. Developers trust that.
11. 12-week roadmap
Weeks | Work | Output
